Getting started with ggsegverse

Source: vignettes/ggsegverse.Rmd
ggsegverse.Rmd

Neuroimaging analysis often ends with a table of regions and p-values. The hard part is turning that table into a figure your audience can actually read. ggsegverse exists to close that gap — one library() call loads everything you need to go from statistics to publication-ready brain figures in R.

library(ggsegverse)
#> ── ggsegverse ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── 0.0.1.9000 ──
#> ✔ ggseg.formats 0.0.4 ✔ ggseg.meshes 0.0.1
#> ✔ ggseg 2.2.1 ✔ ggplot2 4.0.3
#> ✔ ggseg3d 2.1.2

What you get

ggsegverse attaches five packages, each handling a different piece of the visualization pipeline:

  • ggseg — a ggplot2 geom for 2D brain region plots. If you can build a ggplot, you can build a brain figure.
  • ggseg3d — interactive 3D brain widgets built on Three.js, with snapshot_brain() for static images.
  • ggseg.formats — the brain_atlas and ggseg_atlas data structures that both ggseg and ggseg3d rely on, plus bundled atlases (Desikan-Killiany, FreeSurfer aseg, TRACULA, SUIT cerebellum) and FreeSurfer statistics readers.
  • ggseg.meshes — additional cortical surfaces (pial, white, midthickness, and more) and cerebellar meshes for 3D rendering.
  • ggplot2 — the grammar of graphics that ggseg builds on, so theme(), scale_fill_*(), labs() and friends are ready to use.

You do not need to remember which function lives where. Loading ggsegverse makes them all available.

ggsegverse is about plotting. If you want to build your own atlas from a parcellation, that is the job of ggseg.extra, which you install separately.

A first plot

The ecosystem ships four atlases out of the box: dk() (Desikan-Killiany cortical parcellation), aseg() (FreeSurfer subcortical segmentation), tracula() (white matter tracts), and suit() (cerebellar lobules). These are accessed as function calls that return atlas objects.

A cortical surface plot uses geom_brain():

ggplot() +
  geom_brain(atlas = dk(), show.legend = FALSE)

The Desikan-Killiany atlas rendered with ggseg’s default settings.

The subcortical segmentation works the same way:

ggplot() +
  geom_brain(atlas = aseg(), show.legend = FALSE)

FreeSurfer’s automatic subcortical segmentation atlas.

Mapping your own data

The real value is mapping your data onto brain regions. Say you have cortical thickness values for a subset of regions:

my_data <- data.frame(
  region = c(
    "precentral",
    "postcentral",
    "superiorfrontal",
    "inferiorparietal"
  ),
  thickness = c(2.6, 2.1, 2.8, 2.4)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_brain(
    data = my_data,
    atlas = dk(),
    mapping = aes(fill = thickness),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "A") +
  labs(fill = "Thickness (mm)") +
  theme_brain()

Cortical thickness mapped onto Desikan-Killiany regions.

geom_brain() joins your data to the atlas by the region column. Regions without data stay grey.

Interactive 3D views

For presentations or exploratory work, ggseg3d() gives you a rotatable Three.js widget:

ggseg3d(atlas = dk())

Add a translucent cortical surface for anatomical context around subcortical structures:

ggseg3d(atlas = aseg()) |>
  add_glassbrain(opacity = 0.15) |>
  pan_camera("right lateral")

Finding and installing atlases

The bundled atlases cover the basics, but the ggsegverse r-universe hosts many more — Yeo networks, Schaefer parcellations, Glasser HCP-MMP, Harvard-Oxford, and others.

Browse what is available:

ggseg_atlas_repos()

This queries the ggsegverse r-universe and returns a tibble of atlas packages with their versions and descriptions. Core packages and tools hosted there, like ggseg.extra, are left out. You can narrow the list with a pattern:

ggseg_atlas_repos("yeo")

Installing an atlas

Once you have found what you need, install_ggseg_atlas() handles the r-universe repository setup for you:

install_ggseg_atlas("ggsegYeo2011")

After installation, the atlas is available like any other R package:

library(ggsegYeo2011)
ggplot() +
  geom_brain(atlas = yeo7(), show.legend = FALSE)

Installing everything

If disk space is not a concern and you want the full collection:

install_ggseg_atlas_all()

Checking what you have

installed_ggseg_atlases() lists the atlas packages you have installed, with your local version next to the latest one on the r-universe:

installed_ggseg_atlases()

Keeping things current

ggsegverse_sitrep() gives you a quick diagnostic of the core packages — what is installed, what version you are running, and whether anything is out of date:

ggsegverse_sitrep()

If updates are available, ggsegverse_update() prints the exact pak::pak() call to run. It does not install anything for you:

ggsegverse_update()

Name conflicts

When ggsegverse is attached, it lists any function that a core package masks, or that masks one of its functions. Re-exports of the same function across ecosystem packages, like dk(), are not counted as conflicts. You can re-run the check at any time:

ggsegverse_conflicts()
#> No conflicts detected.

If you prefer ambiguous calls to fail loudly, the conflicted package turns every conflict into an error until you choose a winner.
